readerTitle: Three seconds to stop a stranger: rewriting a café sign
caseNote: 가상 사례 (카페 입간판, 식단 앱 업그레이드 배너) · 적용 레슨으로 새 개념 없이 유닛의 개념 3개(명확성, 기능 vs 혜택, 행동 유도)를 사용
insight: 지나가는 사람이 읽는 문구는 세 가지 질문에 답해야 한다. 이게 뭐지? 나한테 뭐가 좋지? 지금 뭘 하면 되지?
misconception: 간판은 재치 있고 독특해야 눈에 띄고, 우리가 얼마나 좋은 재료를 쓰는지 자랑해야 손님이 들어온다.

sources.text: 이 유닛의 개념 레슨: MKT-04-01 기능 vs 혜택, MKT-04-02 명확성이 재치를 이긴다, MKT-04-05 행동 유도
모든 사례와 문구는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 카페와 앱 사례는 모두 가상입니다. 통계나 연구 수치는 쓰지 않았습니다. '사람들이 간판을 몇 초 본다' 같은 정확한 수치는 근거 없이 쓰지 않으려고 'a glance'로만 표현했습니다. 3번 카드와 takeaway의 'three seconds'는 연구 수치가 아니라 독자에게 권하는 자기 점검 방법입니다.
'Ready in 3 minutes'는 가상 카페의 약속 문구입니다. 6번 카드에서 실제로 지킬 수 있는 약속만 쓰라고 한계를 다룹니다.
relatedLessonIds는 2개로 제한되어 MKT-04-02와 MKT-04-01만 넣었습니다. 레슨에서는 MKT-04-05(행동 유도)도 함께 사용합니다.

cards.title: Three seconds to stop a stranger
body: A sandwich board outside a small café reads: *"Bean There, Done That. An artisanal third-wave experience."*
The owner loves it. Hundreds of commuters walk past it every morning. A few smile. Very few stop.

image.label: Commuters walking past a café sandwich board with a pun on it
image.brief: 아침 출근길 보도. 작은 카페 앞 칠판 입간판에 손글씨로 "Bean There, Done That" 문구. 사람들이 휴대폰을 보며 빠르게 지나가고 한 명만 살짝 웃으며 힐끗 봄. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Pick the new main line.
body: You run this café. You can change one main line on the board, big enough to read from across the street. Which do you pick?

options.text: Keep "Bean There, Done That", just in bigger letters
options.feedback: Bigger letters help people see it, not understand it. **Clarity beats cleverness:** the pun only works for people who already know you're a café.
Clear and true, but these are **features**. A commuter in a hurry cares less about how the beans are roasted than about what they get.
Plain words say what you sell, and the time says what a rushing commuter gains. You trade some charm for being understood at a glance.

cards.title: A glance has to answer three questions.
body: A person walking past gives a sign a glance, not a read. In that glance the sign must answer: **What is this? What's in it for me? What do I do now?**

The old board answers none. "Bean There" is a joke you only get once you know it's a café. "Third-wave" is a word coffee fans use. Most commuters don't. The owner wrote for people who already love the place, not for the strangers walking by.

cards.title: One line for each question.

image.label: Before and after: the old pun sign next to the plain three-line sign
image.brief: 입간판 두 개를 나란히 비교. 왼쪽 'Before': "Bean There, Done That / An artisanal third-wave experience". 오른쪽 'After': "Hot coffee & pastries / Ready in 3 minutes / Order at the window →". 오른쪽의 세 줄 옆에 작은 태그 'What it is', 'Why me', 'What to do'. 로고 없음.

breakdown.label: What is this?
breakdown.detail: Clarity: plain words a stranger gets at a glance

breakdown.label: What's in it for me?
breakdown.detail: Benefit: what a commuter gains, not how the beans are made

breakdown.label: What do I do now?
breakdown.detail: Call to action: one clear next step

cards.callout: Nothing clever is left. Every word does a job.

cards.title: Now write the last line.
body: The board now says what you sell and why it's quick. The bottom line tells people what to do next. Which works best?

options.feedback: Warm, but vague. A commuter still doesn't know if there's a queue inside or how long it takes. A **call to action** works best when the step is specific.

options.text: "Order at the window. Tap to pay."
options.feedback: One concrete step that also answers the hidden worry: *will this slow me down?* You give up a friendly tone for a clear path to the counter.
It asks for an action, but not the one that sells coffee this morning. Two different calls to action compete, and the sale usually loses.

cards.title: Plain must also be true.
body: Cleverness isn't banned. Once the plain line does its job, a pun can sit underneath in small letters for the people who stop. Regulars may enjoy it.
But every promise must hold. If "ready in 3 minutes" becomes ten at rush hour, the sign creates disappointed customers. Write only what you can deliver on your worst morning.
And any sign is a guess. Try it for a week and count how many people stop.

cards.title: Now it's an app banner.
body: Your meal-planning app shows free users a banner: *"Pro: powered by our new SmartChef AI engine."* Few tap it. Which rewrite uses what you just practiced?

image.label: Phone screen with an upgrade banner at the top of a recipe app
image.brief: 스마트폰 화면, 레시피 앱 상단에 가로 배너 하나. 배너 문구 자리는 비워 두고 버튼 모양만 표시. 플랫한 일러스트, 실제 앱이나 브랜드 로고 없음.

options.text: "Plan a week of dinners in 5 minutes. Try Pro free →"
options.feedback: Clear about what it does, framed as a **benefit** (time saved), with one next step. It's the café sign's three lines, squeezed into one banner.

options.text: "Pro: AI engine, 10,000 recipes, smart grocery lists"
options.feedback: More concrete than before, but it's a list of features. Users have to work out for themselves what their evenings would gain.
Catchy, but cleverness wins over clarity here. It doesn't say what Pro does or what to tap.

cards.title: Say what it is, why it helps, and what to do.
body: You used three ideas from this unit: **clarity beats cleverness** (what it is), **features vs benefits** (what the customer gains) and **calls to action** (one next step).
**Try it today:** stand where a customer first sees your sign, menu or homepage. Look for three seconds. Can you answer all three questions?
